title: Scaffold or Furniture?
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart examines the evidence base for SEND interventions, noting that many widely used approaches either lack reliable evidence of effectiveness or have been shown to produce no meaningful improvement in outcomes—yet appear routinely in provision maps, IEPs, and TA timetables. The critical question Hart raises is not whether an intervention appears to help a child, but what mechanism is actually producing the observed effect. If a child seems calmer when a familiar object is present, the mechanism may be relational containment rather than sensory regulation; if engagement improves with visual supports, the mechanism may be predictability rather than cognitive scaffolding. Some observed benefit may simply reflect the effect of additional warm adult attention, with the specific tool being largely incidental. Hart introduces a reframe built on a definitional claim: a scaffold is by nature temporary, with a removal plan and parallel capacity-building. If no such plan exists and the intervention has been in place indefinitely, it has stopped being a scaffold—it has become furniture. The students receiving the most intensive provision are precisely those who can least afford for that provision to be ineffective, making rigorous examination of mechanisms a moral priority.
points: * The evidence base for many common SEND interventions is weaker than schools assume; widely used approaches appear in provision maps and IEPs despite lacking evidence of effectiveness or positive trials. * The central question is not 'Does this appear to help?' but 'What mechanism is producing the effect?'—because the mechanism determines the correct response and whether the intervention is genuinely targeting the underlying need. * Some apparent benefit from SEND interventions may be the effect of additional warm adult attention—not the specific tool—with the activity or object being largely incidental. * A scaffold must have a removal plan and parallel capacity-building; without these, it has become permanent furniture—part of the environment rather than a developmental bridge toward independence. * The students receiving the most intensive provision are those who can least afford for that provision to be ineffective—making rigorous examination of mechanisms a moral priority, not just a technical one.
quotes: The students who receive the most intensive provision are those who can least afford for that provision to be ineffective and so our decision making not only of what to start, but also what to stop and when, matters.
When something appears to be helping a child, when they seem calmer, more engaged or more willing to participate, that observation is real. The question is what is actually producing the effect.

If a child is less anxious because a familiar object is present, the mechanism may be containment not sensory regulation. If a child engages more readily when a visual support is in place, the mechanism may be predictability not cognitive scaffolding.
Some of what we observe as benefit may be the effect of additional attention of an adult that matters to the child, not the intervention that structures it.

A scaffold has to be temporary. Its purpose is to enable access to something the child cannot yet reach independently, while the underlying capacity is developed by other means. A scaffold has to have a removal plan.
